claims.value: Side A (French), its own figures: Koch's order of battle of the Army of Italy at the time of 18 October 1805 (pièce justificative VI) gives Gardanne's 1st division of the right wing as 12 battalions and 3 squadrons, 6,066 combattants with 5 guns, and Duhesme's 4th division of the left wing as 13 battalions and 3 squadrons, 6,824 combattants with 6 guns. Duhesme's report of 19 October says that the voltigeurs of the 1st and 4th divisions under Generals Compère and Camus, supported by a brigade of Gardanne's, opened the attack; that his own division stood half in reserve before the bridgehead and half in Verona behind the bridges; and that the other 3 divisions and the grenadier division took no part.
claims.rationale: Side A's return and a participant's report, both printed by Koch and read from the page images. The order of battle states the army as it stood at the time of 18 October, so it does not show how many of these men crossed; Duhesme's report, an interested account, describes how the two divisions were used. Masséna placed these divisions for the crossing (claim side-a-command), so the claim is tagged commander_created. English renderings (ours): 'order of battle of the Army of Italy at the time of 18 October 1805'; 'right wing. 1st Gardanne'; 'total 12 [battalions] 3 [squadrons], giving 6,066 combatants with 5 pieces of ordnance'; 'left wing. 4th Duhesme'; 'total 13 3, giving 6,824 combatants with 6 pieces of ordnance'; the report's dateline, 'the 27 vendémiaire year XIV (19 October 1805)'; Duhesme, 'Marshal Masséna, commander-in-chief of the Army of Italy, having had the petard attached to the gate that closed the bridge over the Adige below the old castle of Verona, and having given the signal for the fight, the voltigeurs of the 1st and 4th divisions, under the orders of Generals Compère and Camus, at once rushed on the Austrian posts that sought to defend the outlet of this bridge, killed them or took them prisoner, and, supported by a brigade of General Gardanne's, advanced on the enemy redoubts with impetuosity, taking the guns that defended them and part of the troops shut up in them'; 'General Duhesme's division had meanwhile been placed half in reserve before the bridgehead, which, traced at once by General Chasseloup of the engineers, was rising with great speed, and the other half in the town of Verona, behind the bridges of the Adige'; 'the 3 other divisions and that of the grenadiers, formed a few days earlier, took no part in this affair'.

claims.value: Masséna commanded side A and planned the crossing: he fixed the night of 17 October for it, meaning to draw the Austrians' attention from the stone bridge of Verona by strengthening the cordon from Zevio to Legnago and by a feigned crossing by Verdier at Becca Civetta, to cross under the protection of Castel Vecchio and to build a bridgehead on the left bank. He went to Castel Vecchio and climbed its right-hand tower, and Duhesme's report says he had the petard attached to the gate that closed the bridge and gave the signal. General Solignac and the engineers led the sappers onto the bridge; General Compère attacked at the head of the first line (Koch). The voltigeurs of the 1st and 4th divisions under Generals Compère and Camus, supported by a brigade of Gardanne's, took the Austrian posts and redoubts, and a charge Gardanne ordered drove the Austrians from their entrenched posts and loopholed houses. When an Austrian column attacked side A's left, the commander-in-chief had Duhesme support Gardanne with a battalion of the 1st of the line, and a battery General Lacombe Saint-Michel had placed on the right bank took the column in flank (Duhesme). Masséna had a bridgehead traced behind Gardanne's division as soon as it had crossed (Koch, Angeli), traced by General Chasseloup (Duhesme); his intention, Duhesme writes, was to confine himself to establishing it.
claims.rationale: Decisions at the engagement from Koch's narrative, an account written from Masséna's papers, and Duhesme's report, an interested account (page images except the passages marked OCR below), with Angeli's agreement on the bridgehead (OCR). English renderings (ours): Koch, 'Masséna fixed the night of 17 October for this movement. His plan was to divert the Austrians' attention from the stone bridge of Verona by reinforcing the cordon from Zevio to Legnago, to have Verdier carry out a feigned crossing at Becca Civetta as a diversion, to make the crossing under the protection of Castel Vecchio, and to establish a bridgehead to give himself a point of support on the left bank'; 'he went on foot to Castel Vecchio and climbed the right-hand tower, which faces the enemy' (OCR); 'General Solignac, the colonel of engineers Sorbier (OCR 'S(ybier') and Captain ... rush onto the bridge' (OCR); 'General Compère (OCR 'Cotetm pare') attacked at daybreak at the head of the first' (OCR); Duhesme, as in claim koch-side-a, and 'a vigorous charge that General Gardanne had made there forced them successively from the entrenched posts and loopholed houses'; 'when the general-in-chief judged it proper to have him supported by General Duhesme, who went there first with a battalion of the 1st regiment of the line commanded by Colonel Desgraviers'; 'taken in flank by the battery that General Lacombe Saint-Michel had had placed on the right bank of the Adige'; Koch, 'that the marshal had a dovetail bridgehead traced behind it' (OCR); Angeli, 'immediately after the division Gardanne had passed the bridge, Masséna had begun the building of a bridgehead' (OCR); Duhesme, 'the intention of the Marshal being to keep to the establishment of this bridgehead'.

claims.value: Side B's troops at Verona were Vukassovich's division of Bellegarde's right wing; Koch calls Vukassovich charged with the defence of this part of the river. Vukassovich brought up battalions of Auffenberg and the Ferdinand hussars from Avesa and Quinzano and led them in a counterattack, which at first threw side A back toward the bridge; a flank attack that Oberst Kéler had been ordered to make with the whole 2nd Banal regiment he made with only part of it; later in the day a battalion of St. Georger Grenzer, advancing from S. Michele on Bellegarde's order, struck side A in the rear and, with the regiment Auffenberg, forced it back (Angeli). The Archduke was not on this part of the field: that evening he marched with the centre against Verdier's crossing. Angeli says the Archduke was highly displeased that, contrary to his definite orders, a pointless and disadvantageous engagement had been accepted; for this evident misreading of his task he relieved Vukassovich of his command, Prince Rosenberg taking his place on the 23rd, and removed Oberst Kéler of the 2nd Banal regiment on the 24th.
claims.rationale: Side B's decisions as Angeli gives them, from Vukassovich's report and other Austrian files (source note 52), with Koch's description of Vukassovich's charge; read from the page images except the counterattack, Kéler's flank attack and the St. Georger battalion (OCR). Angeli's verdict is his own judgment, not a measured effect. claims.value: Bodart describes Verona as a town and fortress on the Adige in Venetia. Near the Porta San Giorgio the Adige, turning west, forms the peninsula of Campagnola, whose neck adjoined Austrian territory; it was swept by the guns of Castel Vecchio and of the bastion San Zeno, which Koch calls a favourable point for the crossing. The salient measures 1,200 to 1,500 m north to south and 600 to 800 m east to west; Borgo San Giorgio, at the back of the bend and at the foot of the hills, is commanded by the hamlets of San Leonardo and Tagliaferro on a spur of the hills; the bend is laid out in gardens and dotted with many isolated houses (Koch). Angeli calls the ground exceptionally favourable to the undertaking: a peninsula cut by many ditches and covered with trees and villas. Both describe fog that morning: Koch counts it and the ground covered with trees, vines and hedges and cut by ditches as the first obstacles, and Angeli calls the ground very broken and covered.

claims.value: Side B misread the attack. Koch says the Archduke, deceived by Verdier's feint, sent 39 battalions and 24 squadrons of the centre in three columns against Verdier, and that side A's lack of success against Veronetta kept him in his error until the night's reports led him to countermand them. Angeli says the Archduke could reach no sure conclusion about side A's first movements, especially Verdier's, because confused, exaggerated and often false outpost reports made any disposition impossible; once the reports of the 18th had come in he was reassured that the position of Caldiero could stop an advance from Verona, and he marched with 41 battalions and 17 squadrons of the centre to Ca del Selle to attack on the 19th. At the bridge itself, which could be watched by day, side B pushed forward only a small post at night. Side B's headquarters took the actions of the 18th and 19th for the opening of Masséna's long-expected offensive.
claims.rationale: Side B's information as both accounts give it (page images, except Angeli's sentences on the outpost reports and the bridge post, OCR, whose numbers are not restated). claims.value: Masséna's aim was to win a secure crossing of the Adige. Angeli says that with the news from Germany favourable it mattered all the more to him to keep the Austrian army in Italy from any diversion through the Tyrol, and that he acted in the sense of a letter from Napoleon; not feeling strong enough to combine the crossing with a decisive blow, he meant at first only to force the bridge at Castel Vecchio and hold side B off until a regular bridgehead secured it. Koch gives the plan as a diversion, a crossing under the protection of Castel Vecchio and a bridgehead as a point of support on the left bank, and Duhesme writes that Masséna's intention was to confine himself to establishing the bridgehead.
claims.rationale: Aims of side A's commander at this engagement, from Angeli (OCR) and Koch and Duhesme (page images). Napoleon's letter was not read and the passages do not give its terms. English renderings (ours): Angeli, 'and it was now all the more important for him to keep the Austrian army in Italy from any diversion through the Tyrol. claims.value: The Archduke did not mean to stop Masséna's crossing at any price, so the Adige below Verona was held only by warning posts (Angeli); he regarded Veronetta and Legnago as outposts only and had ordered their commanders to evacuate them if seriously attacked (Koch). claims.value: Side A attacked: it forced the bridge at Castel Vecchio, took the Austrian posts, redoubt and flèches before S. Giorgio and pushed on to the heights beyond, and attacked Veronetta. Side B counterattacked to regain the position: Vukassovich led battalions of Auffenberg and hussars from Avesa and Quinzano in a counterattack (Angeli), a column attacked side A's left flank (Duhesme), and later a battalion sent by Bellegarde struck side A's rear (Angeli).
claims.rationale: Both sides' accounts describe side A taking the offensive. Side B's attacks were counterattacks to restore its own position at S. Giorgio, which under the brief do not make it an attacker. Masséna, side A's commander at the engagement, chose the night, the place and the plan (claim side-a-command), so the posture is tagged commander_created; Angeli places the operation in the sense of a letter from Napoleon (claim side-a-objectives), whose terms were not read. claims.value: Both sides fought from works. Side B: the Archduke had a line of entrenchments built on Campagnola 1,000 m from Castel Vecchio, a closed redoubt and three flèches with a demi-lune (Koch), or a redoubt about 1200 paces from the castle and three flèches among the foremost houses (Angeli); Veronetta had a bastioned enceinte flanked by towers, partly demolished, and two dismantled old forts (Koch); its bridges were closed by tambours, each with 1 gun, and a crenellated wall covered the passage along the bank (Angeli). Duhesme's report has side A take the enemy redoubts with their guns, force the entrenched posts and loopholed houses, and meet flanking fire from the fortifications of S. Giorgio; Angeli has the fire of the works check side A and the redoubt hold out until surrounded. Side A: its guns fired from Castel Vecchio, flanked by four towers with ditches, whose front facing Austria had recently been put in a state of defence, and from the intact bastion of Spain, whose heavy guns swept the left bank (Koch); Angeli says side A held its ground only with the help of the superior fire from the fortress. The bridges were barricaded at both ends (Koch).
claims.rationale: Koch, Duhesme and Angeli agree on the works, so they are recorded in one claim (page images, except the passages marked OCR). Side A's part is its artillery in the castle and on the bastion, while its infantry attacked in the open; side B's infantry fought from the works and Veronetta. The permanent works (the castle, the bastion, Veronetta's walls and forts) are inherited, while the Campagnola works were built on the Archduke's orders before the action, not by side B's commander at this engagement, so the claim is tagged unresolved, as for B365a. Angeli's footnote says the Archduke had ordered these works not to be occupied (claim side-b-objectives), yet both accounts have them manned. English renderings (ours): Koch, 'but foreseeing the advantage we could draw from it, Archduke Charles had had raised there, 1,000 metres from Castel Vecchio, a line of entrenchments consisting of a closed redoubt at Artaglia and of three flèches thrown up between the houses of the suburb and the enceinte of Veronetta, with a demi-lune to defend their front and flanks'; Angeli, 'the suburb of S. Giorgio was covered by a redoubt built close to the Adige about 1200 paces from Castel Vecchio and by three flèches distributed among the foremost houses, which closed the plain of Campagnola at its neck'; Koch, 'three bridges, closed and barricaded at both ends, joined the Italian town to the Austrian town. Both had a bastioned enceinte flanked by large towers, but partly demolished by us during the last war, and two old forts, though dismantled, protected Veronetta'; Angeli, 'in Veronetta the bridge at Castel Vecchio was in any case closed off; the other three, which carried the communication with Verona, were closed by tambours and each received 1 gun for its defence. A crenellated wall secured the passage along the bank'; Duhesme, 'the left resting on the fortifications of Saint-Georges of Veronetta, where they had infantry and guns whose fire took our troops in flank'; and as in claim side-a-command; Angeli, 'an extremely strong fire from the Austrian works, in which the guns of Veronetta also took part, checked the advance of the French, who held their ground in the very broken and covered ground only with the help of the superior artillery fire from the fortress' (OCR); 'only the redoubt still held out and, with its ... (OCR) guns, did the enemy considerable damage until the garrison, completely surrounded, had to lay down its arms' (OCR); Koch, 'Castel Vecchio, flanked by four towers with ditches and placed on the right bank at the head of the salient of Campagnola, commanded the peninsula'; 'and quite recently the front facing the Austrian states had been put in a state of defence'; 'the bastion of Spain alone had remained intact in the Italian town, and guns of heavy calibre there swept the left bank of the Adige'; 'the artillery placed on the curtain of Castel Vecchio holds the enemy in check' (OCR); Angeli, 'shortly afterwards ... (OCR) heavy guns opened from the castle a violent fire of shell and canister on the Campagnola, which drove back the Austrian posts and kept the space before the bridge clear' (OCR).

open_questions: Deferred: Koch's narrative of the dispositions, the crossing and the counterattack (t. V, pp. 85-88) and Angeli's (Bd. III, pp. 87, 89-91) were read only in the OCR; the reports Angeli cites (source note 52: Vukassovich's of 21 October, Major Geppert's and Captain Hundt's, Kriegsarchiv F. A. X) and Archduke Maximilian's diary; Masséna's own report of the action; Bodart's officer-loss table (not transcribed). Figures seen only in the OCR and not restated in values: the hours of the petard and of the St. Georger battalion's arrival; the numbers of voltigeur companies, line regiments and heavy guns in Angeli; the battalion numbers of Auffenberg's counterattack and of Kéler's flank attack; the bridge post; the redoubt's guns; Koch's number of Vukassovich's guns; Angeli's lengths of the peninsula in paces.

Most consequential gap: side B's strength in the action. Bodart prints none; Angeli gives the division's strength on 13 October over a 54 km front and the units at S. Giorgio and in Veronetta without a headcount, with Auffenberg's 4 battalions at 1931 men at the deployment; Koch gives companies and battalions. An Austrian return for 18 October in the Kriegsarchiv files Angeli cites (F. A. X) could close it.

Disputes kept as separate claims or recorded in them: side B's loss as 1,200 men with 800 prisoners and 7 guns (Bodart), 1,800 killed, wounded or prisoners with 7 guns and 18 caissons (Koch), 1,500 prisoners with 7 or 8 guns (Duhesme) or 1622 men at S. Giorgio and 76 at Veronetta with 4 guns and half a cavalry battery (Angeli); side A's loss as about 900 with 100 prisoners (Bodart) or 150 dead and 300 wounded (Koch, and Angeli citing Masséna); the garrison of the works (2 companies, Koch; the 1st battalion of Auffenberg, Angeli) and of Veronetta (8 battalions, Koch; troops of Hohenlohe and Coburg, Angeli in the OCR); the centre's march against Verdier (39 battalions and 24 squadrons, Koch; 41 battalions and 17 squadrons, Angeli); the Archduke's order not to occupy the works (Angeli's footnote) against their occupation in both accounts.

Families and dependence: Bodart (a compilation; his sources for this entry were not checked; his 7 guns agree with Koch); Koch (a French history written from Masséna's papers and the war ministry's depots, printing the army's order of battle and Duhesme's report, an interested account); Angeli (an Austrian history written from the Kriegsarchiv files, an interested account commissioned by the Archduke's family; his source note 52 cites Koch, V, 83 (page number read in the OCR), and he gives side A's losses as Masséna's statement, so he is not independent of Koch on side A).
